title: How Much Do House Flippers Actually Make After Taxes? A Real Look at the Numbers
excerpt: House flipping can be highly profitable, but taxes take a bigger bite than most beginners expect. This guide breaks down real after-tax earnings so you know exactly what to plan for.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how much do house flippers actually make after taxes
metaDescription: Wondering how much house flippers actually make after taxes? We break down gross profits, tax rates, and real net earnings with examples.

sections.content: House flipping looks glamorous on TV. Buy a rundown property, renovate it, sell it for a big profit. But when investors ask how much do house flippers actually make after taxes, the honest answer is often more complicated than the highlight reel suggests. Taxes, holding costs, and unexpected repairs can quietly eat away at a profit that looked great on paper. This guide gives you a realistic, numbers-based breakdown so you can plan smarter from deal one.
What Is the Average Gross Profit on a House Flip?

According to ATTOM Data Solutions, the average gross profit on a house flip in the United States was around $66,000 in recent years. That sounds like a strong payday. But gross profit is simply the difference between what you paid for the home and what you sold it for. It does not account for renovation costs, holding costs, closing fees, agent commissions, or taxes. Once all of those expenses come out, the actual take-home number shrinks significantly.

A more realistic figure that investors track is the return on investment, or ROI. The national average ROI on flips has hovered between 25% and 35% of the purchase price before expenses. After expenses, net margins typically fall between 10% and 20% for experienced flippers working efficient markets. Beginners often see thinner margins in their first few deals.
The Real Costs That Shrink Your Profit

Before we get to taxes, you need to understand what eats into your gross profit first. Here is a realistic breakdown for a $200,000 purchase price flip sold for $280,000, giving you an $80,000 gross spread.

items: Renovation costs: $30,000 to $45,000 (use a Rehab Estimator at aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator to build accurate scopes)
Holding costs (mortgage, insurance, utilities for 4-6 months): $6,000 to $10,000
Agent commissions on sale: $11,200 to $16,800 (typically 4-6% of sale price)

sections.content: Add those up and your $80,000 gross profit can realistically shrink to $15,000 to $25,000 before taxes. That is the number most beginners never see coming. And taxes still have not entered the picture yet.

Always build your budget with a 15% contingency buffer on top of your renovation estimate. Unexpected plumbing, electrical, or structural issues are the rule, not the exception. Skipping this step is one of the most expensive mistakes new flippers make.
How House Flipping Profits Are Taxed

This is where house flipping gets expensive for people who do not plan ahead. If you flip a property and sell it within 12 months of purchase, your profit is taxed as ordinary income under short-term capital gains rules. That means you pay the same rate as your regular job income, which can range from 22% to 37% depending on your total earnings for the year.

If you hold the property for longer than 12 months before selling, your profit qualifies for long-term capital gains rates, which are 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your income bracket. Most flippers, however, aim to sell within 3 to 6 months, which means short-term rates almost always apply.
Self-Employment Tax: The Hidden Cost

If the IRS classifies you as a real estate dealer rather than an investor, and that happens when you flip homes regularly as a business, your profits are also subject to self-employment tax of 15.3% on top of your income tax. That is a massive hit. For someone in the 22% income tax bracket who also pays self-employment tax, the combined effective rate on flip profits can easily reach 35% to 40%.
The IRS does not care how hard you swung a hammer. They care how long you held the asset. Planning your tax strategy before you buy is just as important as planning your renovation scope.
A Real After-Tax Example: What You Actually Keep

Let us walk through a complete example. You buy a distressed property in a growing market like Atlanta, Dallas, or Phoenix for $180,000. You see opportunities in all three of those cities at aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga, aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx, and aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az. You sell it six months later for $265,000.

That means on an $85,000 gross spread, the realistic take-home for this flip is around $14,000 after all costs and taxes. Is it still worth doing? Absolutely, especially if you can scale to 4, 6, or 8 flips per year. But it should completely change how you evaluate whether a deal is worth pursuing in the first place.
How Experienced Flippers Protect Their Profits

The investors who consistently keep more of their profits are not necessarily finding better deals. They are managing their tax exposure more strategically. Here are the most effective methods seasoned flippers use.

items: Flip through an LLC or S-Corp to reduce self-employment tax exposure
Deduct all legitimate business expenses including mileage, home office, tools, and software
Work with a CPA who specializes in real estate, not a general tax preparer
Reinvest profits into rental properties to access depreciation deductions
Explore opportunity zone investments to defer or reduce capital gains
Track every receipt from day one so deductions are never missed at tax time

sections.content: Should You Consider Wholesaling Instead?

If the tax burden on flipping feels heavy, wholesaling is worth understanding as an alternative or complementary strategy. Wholesalers assign contracts to buyers for assignment fees typically ranging from $5,000 to $25,000 per deal, with far less capital at risk and no renovation exposure. The profits are still taxed as ordinary income, but the lower overhead means your after-tax return per hour of work can actually be higher. What Profit Margin Should You Require Before Pulling the Trigger?

Given what you now know about taxes and expenses, most experienced flippers require a minimum gross margin of 20% to 25% of the after-repair value before they will move forward on a deal. On a home with an ARV of $300,000, that means they need at least $60,000 to $75,000 in gross spread baked in from the start. Deals that do not hit that threshold simply do not leave enough room for the unexpected costs and the tax bill waiting at the end.

Run your numbers using the 70% rule as a starting point: pay no more than 70% of the ARV minus renovation costs. This built-in buffer is specifically designed to protect your margin even after taxes and unexpected expenses eat into it.

The investors making real money in house flipping are the ones who treat it like a business from day one. They track every dollar, consult tax professionals before the deal closes, and use data-driven tools to find properties with enough margin to survive the real world. The TV version of flipping skips straight from the renovation reveal to a big profit number. The real version includes a tax accountant at the closing table.
